Forensic identity review · Module 03

Which Pump Do You Mean?

Five records all say P-104. That does not prove they describe one pump. In this lesson you will treat matching labels as evidence, not as identity, and decide what can safely be connected.

01
Evidence intake

Five systems, one familiar label

A maintenance planner opens a work order for Pump P-104. The geographic map has P-104 at North Pump Station. The control system has a tag called P104_RUN. A drawing labels a pump P-104. An old spreadsheet lists P-104 at South Booster Station.

The easy move is to join the five records on the label. The responsible move is to ask what evidence establishes that they refer to the same physical asset. A source identifier tells you how one system knows the record. A canonical identifier is useful only after the identity decision has been governed. It is not a magic string that makes the records agree.

Matching names create candidates. Location, equipment characteristics, drawings, dates, and approved crosswalks help prove or reject a match.

Preserve source identifiers, match methods, confidence, effective dates, and the reviewer who approved an equivalence relationship.

Fund identity stewardship as operational control. A false merge can contaminate maintenance, risk, customer exposure, and capital planning at once.

Do not merge yet

Choose what you would do with the spreadsheet row before seeing the other evidence. Then read the board by source, location, equipment signature, and date. The label is intentionally the least useful column.

First decision Evidence judgment

The spreadsheet says P-104 but places it at South Booster Station. What do you do?

02
Adjudication room

Same as, related to, or unresolved?

An identity assertion is stronger than a loose connection. If two identifiers are asserted to be the same entity, statements about either can be combined. That is useful and dangerous.

Sometimes the correct relationship is not “same as.” A control-system tag may monitor a pump. A work order may concern a pump. A photograph may depict a pump. These records relate to the asset without becoming the asset. The match method should state how that conclusion was reached.

The remaining cases belong in a conflict queue. Unknown is a valid state. It is safer than a false equivalence that quietly spreads. Record an effective date when equipment replacement or source changes can alter the match.

Follow the evidence, not the label

The provenance view shows where each candidate came from and who reviewed it. In the lab, assign one of three outcomes: same physical pump, related record, or unresolved conflict. Every choice produces an explanation.

03
Blast-radius test

One false merge changes more than one screen

Suppose the legacy South Booster Station record is merged into the North Pump Station asset. Its 75-horsepower motor, maintenance history, and service area now appear to describe the North pump. A query for open work may return the wrong work order. A risk model may combine two failure histories. A customer-exposure path may attach the wrong zone.

This is the blast radius of identity. Graph connections make useful knowledge travel. They also make bad identity assertions travel.

Run both versions

Switch between held conflict and false merge. Read each downstream consequence in order. Then decide which control stops the error closest to its source.

False equivalence propagation Failure-propagation chain
How to read it: Begin with the identity assertion. Each later card consumes the contaminated result without knowing that the original match was weak.

What the chain proves: Review identity before graph traversal, reasoning, analytics, or agent action can reuse it.

04
Professional record

Create the identity crosswalk and conflict queue

A useful crosswalk records both approval and uncertainty. Include the source system, local identifier, proposed canonical identifier, relationship type, evidence, reviewer, effective date, and status. Do not erase the source identifier after mapping it. You need that lineage when a record changes or a decision is challenged.

Document one approved mapping and one conflict

The artifact is intentionally split. The first half records what can be connected. The second preserves what must not yet be merged. The final review requires evidence and a named decision owner.

Identity FAQ

Questions that arise during matching

Why not use the asset tag as the universal identity?

An asset tag may be reused, mistyped, changed during replacement, or scoped only within one facility. Keep it as evidence and a source identifier. Approve a cross-system mapping only when the utility can support the match.

Can two systems disagree without either being wrong?

Yes. A control system may identify a motor-control tag while the asset system identifies the physical pump. Those records are related, but they are not the same entity. The model should represent the distinction.

Who should approve identity mappings?

The answer depends on the asset and decision. A pump mapping may need the asset steward, an operator familiar with the station, and the geographic or control-system owner. The approval route should be documented rather than assumed.

What happens when a pump is replaced?

The old and new pumps should usually have different physical-asset identities, even if the functional position remains P-104. Model the replacement event and preserve effective dates so historical work stays attached to the correct equipment.

Should a low-confidence match enter the graph?

It can enter as a candidate claim with status, provenance, and restricted use. It should not be promoted to an unrestricted identity equivalence until the required evidence and approval exist.

Evidence boundary

All P-104 records are instructional. The lesson teaches identity governance and RDF relationship distinctions. It does not establish a specific matching algorithm or utility policy.
